opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a really interesting moment, because for a long time in robotics, when we said "simulation," we meant physics simulation: engines like MuJoCo, Bullet, Isaac. You hand-build a model of the world. You specify the geometry, the masses, the friction coefficients, the contact models, and then you integrate the equations of motion forward. That kind of simulation has been enormously useful for us. A lot of the progress in legged locomotion over the past several years came from training policies in simulation and transferring them to real robots, the whole sim-to-real paradigm.

But traditional simulators have a fundamental bottleneck. Someone has to build the world. Every object, every material, every scene has to be modeled by hand, and the physics is only as good as our approximations. Things like deformable objects, liquids, cloth, or the long tail of messy everyday environments are very hard to model accurately. So there's always a gap between the simulated world and the real one, and closing that gap takes a lot of human engineering.

What video generation models like Veo and Sora 2 show is a completely different route to simulation. Instead of writing down the rules of physics explicitly, the model learns from enormous amounts of video what the world tends to look like and how it tends to evolve. When you watch these generated videos, water splashing, objects falling, people interacting with things, they're not perfect, but they capture an intuitive physics that would be extremely hard to hand-engineer. In a sense, these are learned world simulators.

So I think the meaning of simulation is shifting from "a physics engine we program" to "a world model we learn." And for robotics that matters a lot, because the biggest problem we face is data. Robot data is expensive and slow to collect. If you have a model that can imagine plausible futures, "if the robot does this action, what happens next?", then you can use it for training, for evaluating policies, even for planning, without running every experiment on a physical robot.

That said, I don't think it's a simple replacement yet. Video models today are mostly optimized to look plausible to humans, not to be physically accurate or controllable. For a robot, you need action-conditioning: the model has to respond correctly to precise motor commands, stay consistent over long horizons, and respect physics, not just produce something that looks right for a few seconds. There are also hallucinations, objects appearing or disappearing, contacts that don't make sense. A policy trained against those errors could learn the wrong things.

So my view is that the two will converge. Classical simulators give you precision, controllability, and guarantees. Learned world models give you realism, diversity, and scalability across the long tail of the real world. The future simulator for robotics will probably be some hybrid, or eventually a learned model that's action-conditioned, grounded in physical understanding, and trained on both internet-scale video and robot interaction data. When that happens, simulation stops being a narrow engineering tool and becomes something closer to the robot's own imagination, a way to think before it acts. I find that really exciting.

r001.rationale: It describes traditional physics simulation as specifying physical properties and integrating the equations of motion forward.

r002.rationale: It calls video-generation models a different route to simulation and learned world simulators, explaining that their generated videos depict plausible physical events.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think this is actually one of the most interesting shifts I've seen in my whole career working on robotics. Let me try to explain how I think about it.

For a long time, when we said "simulation" in robotics, we meant something very specific. We meant a physics engine: rigid bodies, contact models, friction coefficients, joint limits, all written down as equations and solved numerically. Something like MuJoCo or Isaac Gym or Bullet. The whole point was that you write down the laws of physics as best you can, and the simulator rolls them forward in time. And then we spent years, honestly, fighting the sim-to-real gap. The simulator is never quite right. Contacts are wrong, deformable objects are terrible, fluids are basically impossible, lighting and textures look fake. So we built all these tricks, domain randomization, system identification, and so on, to make policies trained in simulation survive in the real world.

Now with models like Veo and Sora 2, something different is happening. These models are also, in a sense, simulators. If you give them an initial frame and some description of what happens, they produce a plausible future. But they aren't simulating physics from first principles. They've learned the statistics of how the world looks and moves from an enormous amount of video. So the "physics" is implicit, it's whatever regularities exist in the data.

And I think this forces us to broaden what we mean by simulation. I'd say there are now at least two kinds. One is analytical simulation, where the rules are written by humans, and it's precise, controllable, and interpretable, but limited in scope. The other is learned simulation, or what some people call world models, where the rules are learned from data, and it's much more general in what it can cover, but it's harder to control and you can't fully trust it.

What's exciting for robotics is that the learned kind covers exactly the things the analytical kind is bad at. Cloth, food, liquids, cluttered real environments, humans moving around. A traditional simulator basically can't do a robot folding a shirt in a messy living room convincingly. A video model can at least produce something that looks right. Whether it's physically correct in the details, that's a separate question, and today the honest answer is often no. You'll see objects that pass through each other, or a hand that grasps something and the object doesn't quite follow.

So in the near term, I don't think video models replace physics simulators. I think of them more as complementary. You might use a video model to generate the visual richness and diversity, and a physics simulator to enforce the contact dynamics that actually matter for control. Or you use video models as a kind of imagination or planning tool, where the robot can "picture" the consequence of an action, and then verify in a more rigorous way.

The longer-term question, which I find genuinely open, is whether a sufficiently good learned world model just absorbs the physics simulator entirely. If you train on enough interaction data, maybe the model learns contact dynamics well enough that we don't need the hand-written version anymore. Some people believe that strongly. I'm a bit more cautious, mostly because robots care about precise, low-level, high-frequency control, and that's exactly where visual plausibility and physical correctness diverge the most. A video can look perfectly right and still be off by a centimeter, and a centimeter is the difference between a grasp succeeding and failing.

So to summarize: simulation used to mean "a program that encodes physics." Now it increasingly means "anything that can predict the future state of the world." And the big research question for our field is how to get the best of both, the generality of learned models and the precision of analytical ones.

r001.rationale: It describes traditional simulation as writing down physical laws as equations and solving them numerically to roll motion forward.

r002.rationale: It calls video models a kind of simulator because they generate plausible futures, and describes learned simulation as a broader meaning of simulation.

astra-6.text:
I think video generation models broaden what we mean by simulation. Traditionally, a simulator represents the state of a world and uses explicit rules—often physics equations—to calculate how that state changes. With models like Veo and Sora 2, we can ask whether some of those dynamics can instead be learned from observations, and whether video itself can become an interface to a simulated world.

But there is an important distinction between generating a plausible video and simulating the consequences of an action. If I ask a robot to push a cup, I need to know how the cup moves given that particular push. Does it slide, tip over, or collide with something? A video can look convincing without answering those questions reliably.

So, for robotics, the exciting direction is an interactive, action-conditioned world model. The robot takes an action, the model predicts what happens, and the robot can use that prediction to plan or learn. That requires more than visual realism. It requires consistency over time, responsiveness to actions, and predictions that are accurate enough for the task.

I see the opportunity as combining these approaches. Traditional simulation gives us explicit physical constraints and control. Learned models could bring richer environments and behaviors that are difficult to model by hand. The changing meaning of simulation is that we are moving from worlds we explicitly construct toward worlds we can also learn—but we still have to test whether those worlds support useful decisions.

r001.rationale: It says traditional simulators use physics equations to calculate how a world’s state changes.

r002.rationale: It says video can be an interface to a simulated world, but does not identify generating a physically correct-looking video itself as a form of simulation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think video generation models broaden what we mean by simulation. Traditionally, a simulator represents a state of the world and uses explicit rules to calculate how that state changes. With models like Veo and Sora 2, we can learn some of those patterns directly from visual data. You describe a situation, and the model generates a plausible sequence of what happens next.

But there’s an important distinction between generating something that looks plausible and simulating something you can reliably interact with. For robotics, for example, I need to ask: If the robot applies this force or takes this action, what happens? Does the object move consistently? Does the model preserve the consequences of earlier actions? A convincing video alone doesn’t establish that.

So I see these models as opening a new direction for simulation. They could help us represent much richer environments and behaviors, while traditional simulators provide useful physical constraints and control. The exciting question is how to combine those strengths—to build models that can generate realistic worlds and also respond consistently when an agent acts inside them.

r001.rationale: The response says traditional simulators represent states and use explicit rules to calculate changes, but it does not specify solving physical equations.

r002.rationale: It says video models generate plausible sequences and distinguishes plausible video from reliable interactive simulation; it does not say that physically correct-looking video itself can count as simulation.
